A badger is a wild animal — a medium-sized mammal that lives in forests, grasslands, and farmlands across Europe, Asia, and North America. It is related to weasels, otters, and wolverines, though it looks quite different from all of them.

The badger's face is its most famous feature. It is white, with two thick black stripes running from the nose, over the eyes, and all the way back across the head. This bold, unmistakable pattern makes a badger one of the easiest wild animals to identify.

Its body is low, wide, and stocky — like a small dog pressed close to the ground. A full-grown badger is typically about 60–90 cm long (roughly the length of your arm plus your torso) and weighs around 8–12 kg. Its legs are short but extremely muscular, and its front paws carry long, thick claws — the most important tools it has.
What it does — the digging animal

If one word defines the badger's way of life, it is digging. Badgers dig their homes underground. These underground homes are called setts (the British English word; American English often uses "burrows" or "dens"). A sett is not just a hole — it can be a vast network of tunnels and chambers spreading many meters in every direction, with dozens of entrances. Some setts have been dug, expanded, and lived in by successive generations of badgers for over a hundred years.

Badgers are nocturnal, meaning they sleep during the day inside their setts and come out at night to feed and roam.

Badgers are omnivores — they eat both animals and plants, and they are not picky. Earthworms are their absolute favourite food, especially in Europe; a single badger can eat hundreds of worms in one night. They also eat insects, beetles, small mammals, birds' eggs, frogs, berries, roots, and fungi. Their strong claws help them dig up food from the soil just as easily as they dig their homes.

European badgers (found across most of Europe and into Asia) are fairly social animals. They live in family groups called clans, sharing and maintaining a sett together. These clans can include a dozen or more individuals.

American badgers (found across North America) look slightly different — they are flatter, paler, and have a white stripe running only to the middle of the back — and they tend to live alone rather than in groups.

Despite looking slow and round, a badger is remarkably tough and bold. It does not scare easily. When threatened by a predator, it stands its ground, growls, and can fight ferociously. Very few animals will challenge a healthy adult badger. This fearlessness is one of the defining things people associate with badgers.

Why "badger" also became a verb — a helpful note

You asked only about the noun, but it is worth knowing this connection because it deepens your understanding of the word. The verb to badger (meaning to pester someone repeatedly and relentlessly) comes directly from this animal. It originates from an old and cruel practice called badger-baiting, in which dogs were set on a trapped badger again and again. The badger's stubborn refusal to give in — being harassed over and over yet still holding on — gave English the phrase to badger someone, meaning to nag or pressure them without letting up. So even the verb is a portrait of the animal's personality.

Think of the badger as the underground architect of the animal world — a tough, thick-clawed, boldly striped creature that lives inside the earth, fears very little, and has been digging its home in the same spot for generations. It is quiet and hidden by day, industrious and purposeful by night.
